title: Classic Buffer Overflow
cwe_name: Buffer Copy without Checking Size of Input ('Classic Buffer Overflow')
description: The program copies an input buffer into a fixed-size destination buffer without verifying that the input fits. In C and C++ this typically happens with unbounded routines such as strcpy, strcat, gets or sprintf, where the copy length is determined by the source data rather than the destination size. Overflowing a stack buffer can overwrite saved return addresses and adjacent variables.
prerequisites: Attacker-controlled data (network packet, file field, argv, environment variable) reaches the copy
Destination is a fixed-size stack or heap array
Copy length is derived from the source (NUL terminator) instead of the destination capacity
Exploit mitigations such as stack canaries, ASLR or non-executable stacks are absent or bypassable
impact: Arbitrary code execution by overwriting the saved return address or function pointers
Process crash and denial of service
Corruption of adjacent security-relevant variables such as authentication flags
detection_patterns: Calls to strcpy, strcat, gets, sprintf or scanf("%s") with a fixed-size char array destination
char buf[N] declared on the stack and filled from recv(), read() or getenv() data
Loops copying bytes until a terminator with no index bound on the destination
Compiler warnings from -Wall -Wformat-overflow or static analyzers (clang-tidy, Coverity, CodeQL) on these calls
remediation: Use bounded APIs that take the destination size (snprintf, strlcpy where available, fgets) and check for truncation
Validate input length against sizeof(destination) before any copy and reject oversized input
Prefer std::string or std::vector in C++ so storage grows with the data
Compile with -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2, -fstack-protector-strong, PIE and non-executable stacks
Fuzz parsers with AddressSanitizer enabled to find overflows before release

cve_examples.summary: Stack buffer overflow in the Windows RPC DCOM interface (MS03-026), exploited by the Blaster worm

title: Out-of-bounds Write
description: The software writes data past the end, or before the beginning, of the intended buffer. Besides unbounded string copies, common causes are memcpy calls whose length comes from untrusted input, off-by-one loop bounds and miscalculated offsets into heap allocations. Heap out-of-bounds writes corrupt allocator metadata and neighbouring objects and are a frequent root cause of remote code execution.
prerequisites: A length, offset or index used in a write is influenced by external input
The write target is a fixed-size or previously allocated buffer whose size is not rechecked
No runtime bounds checking (plain C arrays, raw pointers, memcpy/memmove)
impact: Remote code execution via corrupted heap metadata, vtable pointers or function pointers
Silent data corruption of adjacent objects
Crash and denial of service
Privilege escalation when the vulnerable code runs in a kernel or setuid binary
detection_patterns: memcpy(dst, src, len) where len is read from a packet or file header and not compared with the size of dst
Loop conditions using <= against an array length, e.g. for (i = 0; i <= n; i++) buf[i] = ...
Pointer arithmetic such as *(p + offset) = v with offset derived from input
Writes after a realloc that may have shrunk the buffer
remediation: Compare every externally derived length with the actual destination capacity before memcpy or memmove
Track buffer size alongside the pointer (struct with ptr and len) and check it at each write
Use std::vector::at(), std::span or std::array in C++ for checked access in parsing code
Build test and fuzzing targets with -fsanitize=address to catch out-of-bounds writes
Consider memory-safe languages such as Rust for new parsers of untrusted data

title: Out-of-bounds Read
description: The software reads data past the end, or before the beginning, of the intended buffer. It typically occurs when a length field supplied by a peer is trusted and used to read or echo back memory without checking it against the amount of data actually received. The bytes read may contain secrets such as private keys, session tokens or heap pointers that defeat ASLR.
prerequisites: The program trusts a declared length or index from the input rather than the received size
Read results are returned to the attacker (echo, error message, response body)
No bounds checking on memcpy source ranges or array reads
impact: Disclosure of process memory including keys, passwords and other users' data
Leak of pointer values that helps bypass ASLR for a follow-up exploit
Crash when the read reaches an unmapped page
detection_patterns: memcpy(out, in + off, claimed_len) where claimed_len comes from the message and is not compared with the received length
Array reads table[idx] where idx comes from input and is only checked for an upper bound or not at all
String functions (strlen, strcpy) applied to buffers that may lack a NUL terminator
Parsers that advance a pointer by a header-specified amount without checking remaining bytes
remediation: Validate declared lengths against the number of bytes actually received before reading
Keep an explicit end pointer or remaining-length counter in parsers and check it before every read
Ensure buffers passed to string functions are NUL-terminated or use length-bounded variants (strnlen, memchr)
Run fuzzers with AddressSanitizer to detect heap-buffer-overflow reads

cve_examples.summary: Heartbleed: OpenSSL TLS heartbeat trusted the payload length and returned up to 64 KB of server memory

title: Use After Free
description: The program continues to use a pointer after the memory it refers to has been freed. If the allocator has reused that memory for another object, reads and writes through the dangling pointer operate on attacker-influenced data. Use-after-free bugs commonly arise from unclear object ownership, callbacks that free their own context, and error paths that free an object still referenced elsewhere.
prerequisites: A pointer to the freed object remains reachable (global, struct field, container, callback)
The attacker can trigger the free and then a later use, often through event ordering
The attacker can influence what gets allocated into the freed chunk (heap grooming)
impact: Arbitrary code execution through hijacked virtual function tables or function pointers
Information disclosure from the reallocated object
Heap corruption and crashes
detection_patterns: free(p) or delete p not followed by setting the pointer to NULL when the pointer outlives the call
Error-handling paths that free an object which the caller also frees or uses
Raw pointers stored in containers or callbacks while ownership is held elsewhere
Iterating a list while a callback inside the loop may remove and free the current node
remediation: Define a single owner for each object and use std::unique_ptr or std::shared_ptr in C++ instead of raw new/delete
Set pointers to NULL immediately after free and check for NULL before use
Use reference counting or deferred freeing for objects shared with callbacks
Test with AddressSanitizer (heap-use-after-free reports) and fuzz event sequences

title: Double Free
description: The program calls free() twice on the same memory address. This corrupts heap allocator metadata, for example by placing the same chunk on a free list twice, so that two later allocations return the same memory. It usually results from duplicated cleanup code across error paths or from two objects both believing they own the same buffer.
prerequisites: Two code paths (normal and error handling) each release the same pointer
Shallow-copied structs share a heap buffer and both are destroyed
The attacker can steer execution into the error path, e.g. by sending malformed input
impact: Heap corruption that can be turned into arbitrary write and code execution
Allocator abort (e.g. glibc 'double free detected') causing denial of service
Two live objects aliasing the same memory, leading to data confusion
detection_patterns: Multiple free() calls on the same variable without reassignment in between
goto cleanup labels where some branches free resources before jumping
Structs copied by value (memcpy or assignment) that contain owned pointers and have destructors
C++ classes holding raw owning pointers without a user-defined copy constructor (rule of three violation)
remediation: Use a single cleanup path and set pointers to NULL after free so that a repeated free(NULL) is harmless
Make ownership explicit: transfer it with std::move and std::unique_ptr rather than copying raw pointers
Delete or implement copy constructors and assignment operators for classes owning heap memory
Run tests under AddressSanitizer or Valgrind to detect attempting double-free

title: NULL Pointer Dereference
description: The program dereferences a pointer that it expects to be valid but which is NULL. Typical sources are unchecked return values from malloc, lookup functions that return NULL when an item is not found, and optional fields in parsed messages. In user space the result is usually a crash; in kernels or environments where page zero can be mapped it has historically led to code execution.
prerequisites: A function that can return NULL (malloc, fopen, getenv, strchr, map lookup) has its result used unchecked
Attacker can force the NULL condition, e.g. by omitting an optional field or exhausting memory
The crash affects a shared service (daemon, kernel, worker pool)
impact: Denial of service by crashing the process or kernel
Possible code execution in kernel context on systems where address zero is mappable
Bypass of logic that never runs because the process terminates mid-transaction
detection_patterns: Use of malloc/calloc/realloc results without a NULL check
Chained access such as find_user(name)->role without checking the lookup result
Pointer checked for NULL after it has already been dereferenced
Parsers that assume optional message elements are always present
remediation: Check every pointer returned by allocation, lookup and parsing functions before use
Return explicit error codes and handle them at each call site
Use references, std::optional or not_null wrappers in C++ to express non-null contracts
Enable static analysis (clang --analyze, -fanalyzer in GCC) that reports possible NULL dereferences

title: Integer Overflow or Wraparound
description: An arithmetic operation produces a value larger than the integer type can hold, so it wraps around to a small or negative number. When the result is used as an allocation size, such as malloc(count * size), the allocator returns a buffer far smaller than the code assumes, and the following loop writes out of bounds. Signed overflow is additionally undefined behaviour in C and C++.
prerequisites: Attacker controls one or more operands (element count, width/height, length field)
The result is used for memory allocation, bounds checks or array indexing
No overflow check precedes the multiplication or addition
impact: Undersized heap allocation followed by heap buffer overflow
Bypassed length checks (e.g. len + header < max passing after wraparound)
Incorrect financial or quota calculations
detection_patterns: malloc(n * sizeof(T)) or malloc(a + b) where n, a or b come from input
Image or media parsers computing width * height * bpp in 32-bit integers
Length checks of the form if (off + len > size) where off + len can wrap
Mixing signed and unsigned types in size calculations
remediation: Check before multiplying: if (n > SIZE_MAX / sizeof(T)) reject
Use calloc(n, size) or reallocarray(), which perform the overflow check internally
Use checked arithmetic builtins such as __builtin_mul_overflow and __builtin_add_overflow
Rewrite bounds checks to avoid wraparound: if (len > size || off > size - len)
Compile tests with -fsanitize=integer or -fsanitize=undefined

cve_examples.summary: Stagefright: integer overflow in Android libstagefright MP4 sample table parsing leading to heap overflow

title: Use of Potentially Dangerous Function
description: The code calls a library function that can be used safely but is easy to misuse in a way that introduces a vulnerability. In C the classic examples are gets (removed in C11 because it cannot be used safely), strcpy, strcat, sprintf, strtok and atoi. The weakness is the choice of API itself, which makes the program's safety depend on every caller getting manual bounds checks right.
prerequisites: The codebase uses banned or high-risk C library functions
Arguments to those functions can be influenced by external input
No coding standard or compiler check prevents their introduction
impact: Buffer overflows when length assumptions are wrong
Silent integer conversion errors (atoi returning 0 on invalid input, no error signalling)
Thread-safety bugs from functions with hidden static state such as strtok or localtime
detection_patterns: Any call to gets(); it has no length parameter and is never safe
strcpy, strcat, sprintf, vsprintf, scanf("%s") on fixed-size buffers
atoi/atol used to parse untrusted numbers instead of strtol with errno and endptr checks
Non-reentrant functions (strtok, localtime, asctime) used in multithreaded servers
remediation: Maintain a banned-function list and enforce it in CI (e.g. a grep check or #pragma GCC poison gets strcpy)
Replace gets with fgets, sprintf with snprintf, strtok with strtok_r, atoi with strtol plus error checks
Treat compiler deprecation warnings for these functions as errors
Wrap remaining legacy calls in reviewed helper functions that enforce bounds

title: Improper Validation of Array Index
description: The program uses an untrusted value as an array index without verifying that it lies within the array's valid range. A common mistake is checking only the upper bound with a signed integer, which lets negative indices pass and access memory before the array. In memory-unsafe languages this becomes an out-of-bounds read or write; in managed languages it causes unhandled exceptions.
prerequisites: An index, slot number or enum value is taken from a request, file or IPC message
The index is a signed type, or only one side of the range is checked
The array is accessed without runtime bounds checking
impact: Out-of-bounds write enabling code execution (e.g. overwriting a function pointer table entry)
Out-of-bounds read disclosing memory
Crash or ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException causing denial of service
detection_patterns: handlers[cmd]() or table[idx] where cmd/idx come from input
Checks like if (idx < MAX) with idx declared as int, missing idx >= 0
Indices validated against a different array length than the one accessed
Values from switch-less enum casts used directly as indexes
remediation: Check both bounds: 0 <= idx && idx < length, or use an unsigned type plus an upper bound
Derive the bound from the array itself (sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0]) or arr.length) rather than a separate constant
Use checked accessors such as std::vector::at() or std::array::at() for untrusted indices
Map external identifiers to internal indices through a lookup table instead of using them directly

title: Race Condition
cwe_name: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization ('Race Condition')
description: Two or more concurrent operations access a shared resource and at least one modifies it, without synchronization that guarantees a consistent order. In web applications the typical case is a read-modify-write of a balance, stock count or coupon usage counter, where parallel requests all read the same old value. Attackers exploit this by sending many identical requests at the same moment.
prerequisites: Shared state (database row, cache key, in-memory variable) is read and then written in separate steps
Multiple workers, threads or processes handle requests concurrently
The attacker can issue parallel requests, e.g. via HTTP/2 multiplexing or scripted clients
impact: Double spending of account balance, gift cards or vouchers
Exceeding limits such as one-per-user offers or inventory counts
Corrupted data structures and inconsistent application state
detection_patterns: SELECT balance followed by UPDATE balance = <computed value> without a transaction lock
ORM code like obj.count = obj.count + 1; obj.save() in request handlers
Shared in-memory dicts or counters modified by threads without a lock
Go maps or variables accessed from multiple goroutines (reported by go test -race)
remediation: Perform the update atomically in the database: UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ? AND balance >= ?
Use row locks (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) or SERIALIZABLE transactions for multi-step updates
Use unique constraints or idempotency keys so duplicate operations fail
Protect in-process shared state with mutexes or use atomic types
Load-test critical flows with parallel requests to verify the invariant holds

vulnerable_example.code:
def withdraw(conn, account_id, amount):
    bal = conn.execute("SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id=?",
                       (account_id,)).fetchone()[0]
    if bal >= amount:
        conn.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance=? WHERE id=?",
                     (bal - amount, account_id))
        conn.commit()

secure_example.code:
def withdraw(conn, account_id, amount):
    cur = conn.execute(
        "UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? "
        "WHERE id = ? AND balance >= ?",
        (amount, account_id, amount))
    conn.commit()
    if cur.rowcount != 1:
        raise InsufficientFunds()

cve_examples.summary: Dirty COW: race condition in the Linux kernel copy-on-write handling allowing writes to read-only memory mappings

title: Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU)
description: The program checks a property of a resource, such as a file's permissions or existence, and later uses the resource assuming the property still holds. Between the check and the use, an attacker can replace the resource, most commonly by swapping a file for a symbolic link. The flaw is classic in setuid programs and in code that writes to shared directories like /tmp.
prerequisites: The check and the use refer to the resource by path rather than by an already-open handle
The attacker can modify the path in between (writable directory, shared /tmp)
The program runs with higher privileges than the attacker
impact: Privileged write to arbitrary files such as /etc/passwd via a symlink swap
Disclosure of files the attacker could not normally read
Bypass of permission checks performed with access()
detection_patterns: access(path, W_OK) or os.access() followed by open(path)
os.path.exists(path) followed by open(path, 'w') to create a file
stat() or lstat() on a path followed by a separate open, chmod or chown of the same path
Predictable temporary file names in /tmp created without O_EXCL
remediation: Open the resource once and perform checks on the file descriptor (fstat) instead of the path
Create files atomically with O_CREAT | O_EXCL, and use O_NOFOLLOW to refuse symlinks
Use mkstemp() or Python's tempfile module rather than building temporary paths by hand
Drop privileges (seteuid) to the requesting user before opening instead of emulating checks with access()

title: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
description: The software does not properly control how much of a limited resource, such as CPU, memory, disk, file descriptors or connections, a request can consume. A single request or a small number of them can then exhaust the resource and deny service to everyone. Typical examples are reading an entire request body into memory with no size cap, and regular expressions with catastrophic backtracking.
prerequisites: The endpoint is reachable by unauthenticated or low-privilege users
Processing cost scales with an attacker-controlled input size or complexity
No server-side limit on body size, processing time or concurrent work
impact: Service outage through memory exhaustion (OOM kill) or CPU saturation
Disk exhaustion that also breaks logging and other services on the host
Increased cloud costs from autoscaling under attack
detection_patterns: Body parsers configured without a size limit, or code reading request.body / req.on('data') into an unbounded buffer
Regular expressions with nested quantifiers like (a+)+ or (.*a){n} applied to user input (ReDoS)
Missing server timeouts (Go http.Server without ReadTimeout/WriteTimeout, no proxy timeouts)
Uploads written to disk without per-file and per-user quotas
remediation: Set explicit request body limits in the framework and at the reverse proxy (e.g. client_max_body_size in nginx)
Configure read, write and idle timeouts on servers and outbound clients
Avoid backtracking-prone regexes or use a linear-time engine such as RE2
Run workers with memory and CPU limits (cgroups, container limits) so one request cannot take down the host
Stream large payloads instead of buffering them fully

cve_examples.summary: HTTP/2 Rapid Reset: request creation and cancellation via RST_STREAM consumed server resources, enabling record-size DDoS attacks

references.title: OWASP Denial of Service Cheat Sheet

title: Allocation of Resources Without Limits
cwe_name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling
description: The software allocates resources on behalf of a caller without imposing a limit on how many or how large they may be. In APIs this most often appears as list endpoints that honour any client-supplied page size, batch endpoints with no maximum item count, or per-user objects (sessions, API keys, uploads) that can be created without quota.
prerequisites: A parameter such as limit, page_size, ids[] or batch length is fully controlled by the client
The backend translates the request directly into a database query or allocation of that size
No per-user or per-tenant quotas are enforced
impact: Database and application memory exhaustion from queries returning millions of rows
Slow responses for all users while large queries run
Storage exhaustion from unlimited object creation
detection_patterns: Handlers passing request.args['limit'] straight into LIMIT clauses or ORM .limit() calls
List endpoints with no pagination at all (SELECT * FROM table returned as JSON)
GraphQL queries without depth, complexity or result-size limits
Creation endpoints (keys, webhooks, projects) without a count check per account
remediation: Apply a server-side maximum to page sizes and default to a small value when none is given
Use cursor-based pagination for large collections
Cap batch sizes and array lengths in request schema validation
Enforce per-user and per-tenant quotas on created resources
Set statement timeouts on database connections used by request handlers

references.title: OWASP Denial of Service Cheat Sheet

title: Decompression Bomb (Data Amplification)
cwe_name: Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification)
description: The software decompresses input without limiting the size of the output. A small, highly compressed archive (a zip bomb) or a gzip-encoded request body can expand to gigabytes or terabytes, exhausting memory or disk. The danger is that size checks on the compressed upload give a false sense of safety.
prerequisites: The application accepts archives, compressed uploads or Content-Encoding: gzip request bodies
Decompression output is fully buffered in memory or written to disk without a cap
Only the compressed size is validated
impact: Memory exhaustion and process termination
Disk exhaustion on the server or shared volume
Long CPU-bound decompression blocking worker threads
detection_patterns: zipfile.ZipFile(...).extractall() or ZipInputStream loops with no total-size counter
gzip.decompress(data) or zlib.decompress(data) on untrusted input
Trusting the uncompressed size declared in the archive header without enforcing it while reading
Recursive extraction of nested archives
remediation: Decompress in streaming fashion and abort once a maximum output size is exceeded
Limit the number of entries and the total uncompressed size per archive
Reject or cap the compression ratio (e.g. abort above 100:1)
Do not extract nested archives automatically
Run extraction in a worker with memory and disk quotas

vulnerable_example.code:
import zipfile

def import_bundle(path, dest):
    with zipfile.ZipFile(path) as z:
        z.extractall(dest)          # no limit on expanded size

title: Uncontrolled Recursion
description: The software uses recursion whose depth is controlled by input and does not bound it. Deeply nested JSON, XML or YAML documents, self-referencing data and recursive variable expansion can drive the call stack to exhaustion. Depending on the runtime, this produces a stack overflow crash, a RecursionError that kills the request, or unbounded memory use.
prerequisites: A parser or tree walker recurses once per nesting level of attacker-supplied data
No explicit maximum depth is enforced
Self-references or cycles in the data are not detected
impact: Process crash from stack exhaustion (StackOverflowError, segfault in native code)
Denial of service for the whole worker if the error is not caught
Excessive CPU and memory consumption during expansion
detection_patterns: Recursive functions over request data such as def walk(node): ... walk(child) with no depth parameter
Custom JSON/XML/YAML parsers or template expanders that recurse on nesting
Recursive lookups or substitutions that may reference themselves
Catch-all handlers that swallow RecursionError and retry the same input
remediation: Pass a depth counter through recursive calls and reject input beyond a fixed maximum
Convert recursion to iteration with an explicit stack for untrusted structures
Detect cycles by tracking visited nodes or expansion keys
Use parser options that cap nesting depth where libraries provide them

cve_examples.summary: Apache Log4j 2 did not protect against uncontrolled recursion from self-referential lookups, causing denial of service

title: Infinite Loop
cwe_name: Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop')
description: The program contains a loop whose exit condition can never be satisfied for some inputs. This often happens in parsers that advance a cursor by a length taken from the input: a length of zero means the cursor never moves. A single crafted message can then pin a CPU core indefinitely.
prerequisites: Loop progress depends on values decoded from input (length fields, offsets, pointers to next record)
Zero, negative or backward-pointing values are not rejected
No iteration cap or timeout on the processing
impact: CPU exhaustion of a worker or thread, eventually making the service unresponsive
Request queues backing up behind the stuck worker
Watchdog restarts and degraded availability
detection_patterns: while (offset < len) loops where offset += field_len and field_len may be 0
Linked structures in files (next-record offsets) followed without cycle detection
Retry loops (while True: try ... except: continue) with no attempt limit or backoff
Loops whose counter type can wrap before reaching the bound
remediation: Ensure every iteration makes forward progress; reject zero or backward offsets
Add a maximum iteration count proportional to the input size
Track visited offsets when following pointers inside data
Bound retry loops with a maximum attempt count and exponential backoff
Apply per-request processing timeouts

title: Insecure Default Initialization
cwe_name: Initialization of a Resource with an Insecure Default
description: A resource is created or shipped with a default setting that is insecure, and the system relies on administrators to change it. Examples include services binding to 0.0.0.0 with authentication disabled, default admin credentials, storage buckets created public, and permissive CORS. Because many deployments never change defaults, the weakness is reliably exploitable at scale.
prerequisites: The software or deployment template ships with an insecure default value
Operators deploy without hardening or without being warned
The affected service is reachable from an untrusted network
impact: Unauthenticated access to databases, caches, dashboards or admin interfaces
Mass compromise through internet-wide scanning for known defaults
Data exposure from storage created with public access
detection_patterns: Configuration files or Helm values with auth disabled, default passwords or bind addresses of 0.0.0.0
Code like os.getenv('ADMIN_PASSWORD', 'admin') or SECRET_KEY fallbacks
Docker Compose files publishing database ports (e.g. 5432:5432, 6379:6379) on all interfaces
CORS configured with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * plus credentials, or framework defaults left unchanged
remediation: Make the secure setting the default (authentication on, bind to localhost, private storage)
Fail to start when required secrets are missing instead of falling back to a hard-coded value
Generate unique credentials at install time rather than shipping a shared default
Scan infrastructure-as-code with policy tools to block insecure defaults before deployment

vulnerable_example.code:
services:
  redis:
    image: redis:7.2
    command: redis-server --protected-mode no
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"          # exposed on all host interfaces, no password

secure_example.code:
services:
  redis:
    image: redis:7.2
    command: ["redis-server", "--requirepass", "${REDIS_PASSWORD:?REDIS_PASSWORD must be set}"]
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:6379:6379"  # loopback only

title: Active Debug Code
description: The application is deployed with debugging code or debug modes enabled. Interactive debuggers such as the Werkzeug debugger in Flask allow arbitrary Python execution from the browser, and debug endpoints or backdoor parameters left from development bypass normal controls. These features are intended for local use and are dangerous once reachable from a network.
prerequisites: A debug flag, profiler or diagnostic endpoint is enabled in the production build
The debug interface is reachable by untrusted users
No build-time or deployment check separates development and production configuration
impact: Remote code execution through interactive debug consoles
Authentication bypass via test-only parameters or hard-coded debug users
Leakage of source code, environment variables and stack frames
detection_patterns: app.run(debug=True), DEBUG = True in Django settings, or FLASK_DEBUG=1 in production environment files
Routes such as /debug, /__test, /actuator/* or /admin/eval enabled without authentication
Code branches like if request.args.get('debug') == '1': skip_auth()
Node.js processes started with --inspect bound to a public interface
remediation: Drive debug settings from environment-specific configuration with production defaulting to off
Remove test-only routes and bypass flags from production builds, e.g. via build tags or separate modules
Add a startup assertion that refuses to run with debug enabled when ENV=production
Restrict management endpoints to internal networks and require authentication

vulnerable_example.code:
from flask import Flask
app = Flask(__name__)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(host="0.0.0.0", debug=True)   # Werkzeug console reachable remotely

secure_example.code:
import os
from flask import Flask
app = Flask(__name__)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    debug = os.environ.get("APP_ENV") == "development"
    host = "127.0.0.1" if debug else "0.0.0.0"
    app.run(host=host, debug=debug)
# production: run under gunicorn, never app.run()

title: Protection Mechanism Failure
description: The product does not use, or incorrectly uses, a protection mechanism that would defend against a class of attack. This covers missing defences (no CSRF tokens, no security headers, no rate limit) as well as defences that are present but ineffective because they are disabled, misconfigured or easily bypassed. It is a broad class; more specific CWEs should be preferred when the exact failure is known.
prerequisites: A standard defence for the platform is absent, disabled or configured permissively
The attack class it would prevent is applicable (e.g. browser-based clients for CSRF or clickjacking)
No testing verifies that the defence is active in the deployed environment
impact: Exposure to attacks the mechanism was meant to stop (CSRF, clickjacking, XSS, brute force)
False confidence because a control appears configured but does not take effect
Audit and compliance failures
detection_patterns: Security middleware commented out or disabled (csrf_exempt, helmet() not applied, CSP removed)
Response headers missing Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors or Strict-Transport-Security
Defences applied only in client-side JavaScript
Allow-list checks implemented with substring matching that can be bypassed
remediation: Enable framework security middleware globally and require justification for any exemption
Set security headers centrally at the reverse proxy or application entry point
Enforce controls on the server, never only in the client
Add automated tests or DAST checks that assert headers and CSRF validation are present

title: Dependency on Vulnerable Third-Party Component
description: The product depends on a library, framework or other third-party component that contains a known vulnerability. The weakness is inherited: application code may be correct, yet the bundled component is exploitable. Exposure is usually caused by unpinned or never-updated dependencies and by not tracking transitive dependencies in a software bill of materials (SBOM).
prerequisites: A dependency version with a published vulnerability is included in the build or runtime
The vulnerable code path is reachable from attacker input
There is no automated dependency scanning or update process
impact: Remote code execution through a framework or library flaw
Data breach via a vulnerability the team was unaware of
Rapid mass exploitation once a public exploit is released
detection_patterns: Lockfiles or manifests (pom.xml, package-lock.json, requirements.txt) containing versions listed in advisories (OSV, GitHub Advisory Database, NVD)
Unpinned version ranges such as "*", "latest" or >= without a lockfile
Vendored copies of libraries with no recorded version
Container base images not rebuilt for months
remediation: Run software composition analysis (e.g. OWASP Dependency-Check, npm audit, pip-audit, osv-scanner) in CI and fail on critical findings
Pin versions in lockfiles and update them through automated pull requests (Dependabot, Renovate)
Produce and maintain an SBOM so exposure to a new advisory can be determined quickly
Remove unused dependencies to reduce attack surface

vulnerable_example.code:
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.apache.logging.log4j</groupId>
  <artifactId>log4j-core</artifactId>
  <version>2.14.1</version>   <!-- affected by Log4Shell -->
</dependency>

secure_example.code:
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.apache.logging.log4j</groupId>
  <artifactId>log4j-core</artifactId>
  <version>2.17.1</version>   <!-- patched; kept current by Dependabot -->
</dependency>

cve_examples.summary: Log4Shell: JNDI lookup in Apache Log4j 2 message formatting allowed remote code execution in countless dependent applications
Apache Struts Jakarta Multipart parser RCE; exploited against unpatched deployments including the 2017 Equifax breach

references.title: OWASP Vulnerable Dependency Management Cheat Sheet
OWASP Top 10 2021 A06 Vulnerable and Outdated Components

title: Use of Unmaintained Third-Party Components
cwe_name: Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components
description: The product relies on third-party components that are no longer actively maintained by their authors or vendor. Even if no vulnerability is known today, newly discovered flaws will not be patched, and the component may block upgrades of the language runtime or other dependencies. Abandoned packages are also attractive targets for account takeover by attackers who then publish malicious versions.
prerequisites: A dependency is archived, deprecated, end-of-life, or has had no release for years
No internal owner is responsible for patching or replacing it
The component processes untrusted input or runs with significant privileges
impact: Known-but-unfixed vulnerabilities remain in production indefinitely
Inability to upgrade the runtime (e.g. stuck on an end-of-life Python or Node.js version)
Exposure to malicious releases if the abandoned package's maintainer account is compromised
detection_patterns: Dependencies whose upstream repositories are archived or marked deprecated in the package registry
Runtime or framework versions past their end-of-life date (e.g. Python 2.7, AngularJS 1.x)
Packages with no commits or releases for several years and many open security issues
Forked or vendored libraries with no record of upstream syncs
remediation: Review dependency health (release cadence, maintainer activity, deprecation notices) before adoption and periodically after
Track end-of-life dates for runtimes, frameworks and base images and plan migrations ahead of them
Replace abandoned packages with maintained alternatives or take over maintenance in an internal fork with an owner
Flag deprecated packages automatically in CI (npm deprecation warnings, OpenSSF Scorecard checks)

references.title: OWASP Vulnerable Dependency Management Cheat Sheet
OWASP Top 10 2021 A06 Vulnerable and Outdated Components

title: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere
cwe_name: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere
description: The product imports or executes code that comes from a source outside its control without verifying it. Typical cases are third-party scripts loaded from a CDN without Subresource Integrity, CI pipelines referencing actions by mutable tags, and installing packages whose names are typosquats of popular libraries. If the external source is compromised, the attacker's code runs with the application's privileges.
prerequisites: The application loads scripts, plugins or build steps from a third-party location at build or run time
The reference is mutable (tag, branch, unversioned URL) and not integrity-checked
The third party or its distribution channel can be compromised or impersonated
impact: Injection of malicious JavaScript into every page (card skimming, session theft)
Compromise of CI secrets and build artefacts through a malicious pipeline step
Malware installation via typosquatted or hijacked packages
detection_patterns: <script src="https://cdn..."> tags without integrity and crossorigin attributes
GitHub Actions referenced by tag or branch (uses: some/action@v1 or @main) instead of a full commit SHA
Package names that differ by one character from well-known packages (e.g. reqeusts, python3-dateutil)
Dynamic import or require of a URL or path built from configuration or user input
remediation: Add Subresource Integrity hashes to third-party scripts and stylesheets, or self-host them
Pin CI actions and container images to immutable digests (commit SHA, sha256)
Verify package names and publishers before adding dependencies; use an internal registry or allow-list
Use a Content-Security-Policy that restricts script sources to approved origins

vulnerable_example.code: <script src="https://cdn.example-cdn.com/chart-lib/latest/chart.min.js"></script>

secure_example.code:
<script src="https://cdn.example-cdn.com/chart-lib/4.4.1/chart.min.js"
        integrity="sha384-<base64 hash of the exact file>"
        crossorigin="anonymous"></script>

references.title: OWASP Third Party JavaScript Management Cheat Sheet
OWASP Top 10 2021 A08 Software and Data Integrity Failures

title: Download of Code Without Integrity Check
cwe_name: Download of Code Without Integrity Check
description: The product downloads code or executables from a remote location and runs them without verifying a checksum or signature. The common anti-pattern is piping an installer from curl directly into a shell in a Dockerfile or CI script. A compromised server, DNS hijack or tampered mirror then results in arbitrary code execution inside the build or production environment.
prerequisites: Code is fetched over the network at build, install or update time
No hash pinning or signature verification is applied before execution
The download source or path to it (DNS, mirror, CDN) can be tampered with
impact: Arbitrary code execution in build systems, containers or end-user machines
Persistent backdoors in published images and releases
Theft of CI credentials and deployment keys
detection_patterns: curl ... | sh, wget -O- ... | bash, or iex (iwr ...) in Dockerfiles, CI configs and install docs
Auto-update routines that download and execute binaries without signature checks
pip install or npm install from arbitrary URLs without --require-hashes or lockfile integrity
Download over plain HTTP
remediation: Download to a file, verify a pinned SHA-256 checksum or a vendor signature (GPG, Sigstore/cosign), then execute
Pin installer versions so the expected hash is stable
Use pip install --require-hashes and committed lockfiles with integrity fields
Sign update packages and verify the signature in the updater before installing

vulnerable_example.code:
FROM debian:12-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
RUN curl -fsSL https://example.com/install.sh | sh

secure_example.code:
FROM debian:12-slim
ARG TOOL_VERSION=1.8.2
ARG TOOL_SHA256=<published sha256 for this version>
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl \
 && curl -fsSLo /tmp/tool.tar.gz https://example.com/releases/tool-${TOOL_VERSION}.tar.gz \
 && echo "${TOOL_SHA256}  /tmp/tool.tar.gz" | sha256sum -c - \
 && tar -xzf /tmp/tool.tar.gz -C /usr/local/bin

references.title: OWASP Top 10 2021 A08 Software and Data Integrity Failures

title: Insufficient Logging
description: Security-relevant events such as failed logins, access-control denials, privilege changes and input validation failures are not recorded, or are recorded without enough context to be useful. Without these logs, attacks like credential stuffing go unnoticed and incident responders cannot reconstruct what happened. It is a common reason why breaches are detected late.
prerequisites: Authentication, authorization and administrative actions are implemented without audit logging
Logs are not shipped to central storage or are not monitored
Log retention is too short to cover typical detection delays
impact: Attacks proceed undetected (brute force, enumeration, privilege abuse)
Inability to determine the scope of a breach or which data was accessed
Failure to meet regulatory audit requirements
detection_patterns: Login handlers that return an error on bad credentials without logging the attempt
Authorization checks that raise 403 with no audit record
Exception handlers using bare except: pass around security-relevant operations
Logging configured only at ERROR level in production so WARN-level security events are dropped
remediation: Log authentication successes and failures, access denials, privilege and configuration changes with user, source IP, timestamp and outcome
Use structured (JSON) logs and forward them to a central, tamper-resistant store
Define alerts for suspicious patterns such as many failures per account or per IP
Never log secrets, passwords or full tokens in these events

references.title: OWASP Top 10 2021 A09 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures

title: Omission of Security-relevant Information
description: The product records an event but leaves out details that are needed to judge whether it was an attack or to attribute it. Log lines such as 'access denied' without the acting user, target resource or source address are present but forensically useless. This differs from insufficient logging in that the event is logged, but its security context is missing.
prerequisites: Events are logged with fixed messages rather than structured fields
Identity, request and resource identifiers are not propagated to the logging layer
Reverse proxies hide the client address and the application logs only the proxy IP
impact: Inability to attribute malicious actions to an account or source
Correlation across services is impossible without request identifiers
Alerts cannot distinguish one noisy client from a distributed attack
detection_patterns: Log statements like log.warn("permission denied") with no user, resource or action fields
Logged client IP is always the load balancer address because X-Forwarded-For is not handled by a trusted proxy configuration
No correlation or request ID in log records
Timestamps without time zone or with unsynchronized clocks
remediation: Include who (user or service ID), what (action and resource), where (source IP, request ID) and when (UTC timestamp) in every security event
Configure trusted proxy handling so the real client IP is logged
Propagate a correlation ID across services and include it in logs
Use a shared logging schema or vocabulary for security events

secure_example.code:
if !canDelete(user, projectID) {
    slog.Warn("authz_denied",
        "user_id", user.ID, "action", "project.delete",
        "project_id", projectID, "client_ip", clientIP(r),
        "request_id", r.Header.Get("X-Request-ID"))
    http.Error(w, "forbidden", http.StatusForbidden)
    return
}

title: Improper Handling of Exceptional Conditions
description: The software does not handle, or handles incorrectly, exceptional conditions such as failed network calls, missing files, timeouts or unexpected exceptions. A frequent security consequence is failing open: when an authorization service or signature check raises an error, a broad catch block lets the request continue as if the check had passed.
prerequisites: Security decisions depend on calls that can throw or time out
Broad exception handlers swallow errors or return a permissive default
The attacker can induce the error (malformed input, slow dependency, resource exhaustion)
impact: Authorization or validation bypass when the check fails open
Inconsistent state after a partially completed operation
Crashes or hung workers when exceptions are not handled at all
detection_patterns: except Exception: pass or catch (Exception e) {} around authentication, authorization or signature checks
Functions that return True or a default allow value inside an exception handler
Missing timeout and error handling on calls to identity providers or policy services
Unhandled promise rejections in Node.js request handlers
remediation: Fail closed: deny the operation when a security check cannot be completed
Catch specific exception types and handle each deliberately
Use transactions so partial failures roll back
Register a global error handler that returns a generic error and logs details server-side

title: Improper Enforcement of Behavioral Workflow
owasp_api_2023: API6:2023-Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
description: The application expects users to perform actions in a particular order but does not enforce that order on the server. An attacker can call a later step directly, for example confirming an order without paying, resetting a password without completing verification, or skipping a mandatory review. Each endpoint is individually authorized, yet the sequence is not.
prerequisites: A multi-step process is implemented as separate endpoints or pages
Progress through the steps is tracked on the client (hidden fields, URL parameters) or not at all
Later steps do not verify that earlier steps completed successfully
impact: Goods or services obtained without payment
Account takeover by skipping verification steps in recovery flows
Bypass of approval or review stages in administrative workflows
detection_patterns: Step handlers that do not read and check a server-side state field (status, stage) before acting
Hidden form fields such as step=3 or paid=true trusted by the server
State transitions written as unconditional UPDATE status = 'confirmed'
Password reset endpoints that accept a new password without checking a verified token
remediation: Model workflows as an explicit server-side state machine and validate every transition
Store progress server-side bound to the session or the business object, never in client-controlled fields
Use conditional updates (UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'paid') so out-of-order calls have no effect
Write tests that call each step out of order and expect rejection

title: Improper Control of Interaction Frequency
owasp_api_2023: API6:2023-Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
description: The product does not limit how often a user or client can perform an action. Without rate limits, attackers can brute-force passwords or one-time codes, enumerate accounts, abuse SMS or email sending, and automate scarce business actions such as ticket purchases or coupon redemptions. The fix is a deliberate per-identity and per-source frequency policy for each sensitive action.
prerequisites: A sensitive action (login, OTP verification, password reset, message sending) has no request quota
The attacker can automate requests from one or many sources
The action has a small search space or an associated per-use cost
impact: Brute forcing of passwords and short numeric OTP codes
SMS or email pumping that generates direct financial cost
Scalping or exhaustion of limited resources by bots
detection_patterns: Login, OTP and password-reset routes with no rate-limiting middleware or decorator
Rate limits keyed only by IP, allowing distributed attacks against one account
OTP verification without a maximum attempt count per code
Endpoints that send messages or trigger paid third-party calls with no per-user quota
remediation: Apply rate limits per account, per IP and globally on authentication and messaging endpoints
Invalidate one-time codes after a small number of failed attempts
Add progressive delays, CAPTCHA or step-up checks after repeated failures
Return HTTP 429 with Retry-After and log throttling events for monitoring

references.title: OWASP Denial of Service Cheat Sheet

title: External Control of System or Configuration Setting
cwe_name: External Control of System or Configuration Setting
description: One or more system or configuration settings can be changed by an external user who should not control them. Examples include request parameters that select the database, log level, feature flags, or a callback host, and settings APIs that accept arbitrary keys. Altering configuration can disable security features or redirect the application to attacker-controlled resources.
prerequisites: Configuration values are read from request parameters, headers or user-editable records
Settings updates accept arbitrary keys instead of an allow-list
No privilege check restricts who can change system-level settings
impact: Disabling security controls such as authentication, TLS verification or audit logging
Redirecting connections or webhooks to attacker infrastructure
Service disruption by setting invalid or extreme values
detection_patterns: Code like config[key] = value or setattr(settings, key, value) with key from the request
Query parameters such as ?debug=1, ?db=, ?log_level= honoured in production
Admin settings endpoints that lack role checks or accept nested objects unchecked
Environment variables or connection strings assembled from user input
remediation: Separate system configuration from user preferences and never derive system settings from requests
Allow-list the settings users may change and validate each value's type and range
Require administrative authorization and audit logging for configuration changes
Load security-critical settings from read-only, deployment-controlled sources

title: Exposure of Sensitive System Information
cwe_name: Exposure of Sensitive System Information to an Unauthorized Control Sphere
description: The application reveals internal system details, such as software versions, file paths, environment variables, internal hostnames or stack traces, to users who are not authorized to see them. This information does not compromise the system by itself but significantly helps an attacker select matching exploits and map internal infrastructure.
prerequisites: Error pages, headers or diagnostic endpoints are reachable by untrusted users
The application or server returns raw exception details or environment data
Version banners are enabled by default and not disabled
impact: Faster targeting of known vulnerabilities based on exact versions
Disclosure of internal paths, hostnames and IPs that aids lateral movement
Leakage of secrets present in environment variables or configuration dumps
detection_patterns: Server and X-Powered-By response headers with exact versions
Endpoints returning os.environ, phpinfo(), /actuator/env or /server-status publicly
Exception handlers that send traceback or stack trace text in HTTP responses
Health checks that include dependency versions, hostnames or connection strings
remediation: Disable version banners (server_tokens off in nginx, app.disable('x-powered-by') in Express)
Return generic error messages to clients and log details server-side with a correlation ID
Restrict diagnostic and metrics endpoints to internal networks or authenticated administrators
Keep public health checks minimal (status only)

title: Improper Validation of Generative AI Output
cwe_name: Improper Validation of Generative AI Output
description: The product uses output from a generative AI model, such as an LLM, without validating that it is safe and conforms to the expected format before acting on it. Model output can be steered by prompt injection hidden in retrieved documents or user input, so it must be treated as untrusted. Passing it unchecked into HTML, SQL, shell commands or tool calls turns the model into an injection vector.
prerequisites: Model output is passed to an interpreter, renderer or privileged tool (browser DOM, SQL, shell, API call)
Prompts include attacker-influenced content (user messages, retrieved documents, web pages)
No schema, allow-list or encoding is applied to the output
impact: Cross-site scripting when generated text is rendered as HTML
SQL or command injection when generated queries or commands are executed
Unauthorized actions when the model selects tools or arguments outside the user's permissions
Users acting on fabricated facts, references or package names
detection_patterns: innerHTML, dangerouslySetInnerHTML or Markdown rendering of model responses without sanitization
eval(), exec(), subprocess or cursor.execute() called with text produced by an LLM
JSON parsed from model output and used without schema validation
Agent tool calls executed without checking that the tool and arguments are permitted for the current user
remediation: Treat model output as untrusted input: validate against a strict schema (JSON Schema, Pydantic) and reject non-conforming responses
Encode or sanitize output for the target context, e.g. render as text or sanitize HTML with an allow-list
Never execute generated code or queries directly; map outputs to parameterized, pre-approved operations
Enforce authorization on every tool call independently of the model's decision and require human confirmation for high-impact actions

vulnerable_example.code: const answer = await llm.complete(prompt); document.getElementById('chat').innerHTML = answer; // model may emit
